Lecture 19

Random vectors, the covariance matrix and the Jacobian

Deck C, slides 1 to 8 · 29 min read · 12 practice problems

Solutions stay collapsed until you click them.

Where we are. Up to now we've handled one or two random variables at a time. This lecture packs n of them into a single object, a random vector, and uses matrix notation so the algebra stays short. Then it builds vector versions of three tools you already know:

One variable (L1 to L13) Random vector (this lecture)
mean E[X] mean vector E[X]
variance Var(X) covariance matrix CX​
Var(aX+b)=a2Var(X) CAX+b​=ACX​AT
fY​(y)=fX​(h(y))∣h′(y)∣ fY​(y)=fX​(H(y))∣J∣

If you keep the left column in mind, the right column is mostly "the same thing, with matrices". These are exactly the tools L20 needs for Gaussian vectors.

Part A: the slides

Slide 1/36: Random vectors

On the slide. We are now moving from a univariate random variable to multivariate random variables, also called random vectors. An n-dimensional random vector is a column vector X=(X1​,…,Xn​)T whose components Xi​ are scalar-valued random variables defined on the same space (Ω,F,P). Since the components are on the same space, they may be correlated with each other. Example: X=(X1​,X2​)T where X1​=Z1​ and X2​=Z1​+Z2​, where Z1​ and Z2​ are independent standard normal. What is the pdf, cdf, marginals, mean, variance/covariance of X?

Why "the same space" matters. All the components are functions of the same ω, so they can be related to each other. In the example, X1​ and X2​ both contain Z1​: if Z1​ comes out large, both of them get pushed up. So a random vector is really just a tidy way to package several jointly distributed random variables (L10 to L13).

The red question, fully solved. The trick for everything below: write X in terms of the independent Z's and work with those.

Mean. E[X1​]=E[Z1​]=0 and E[X2​]=E[Z1​]+E[Z2​]=0. So E[X]=(0,0)T.

Variances and covariance. Independence of Z1​,Z2​ kills the cross terms:

Var(X1​)=1,Var(X2​)=Var(Z1​)+Var(Z2​)=2,
Cov(X1​,X2​)=Cov(Z1​,Z1​+Z2​)=Var(Z1​)+Cov(Z1​,Z2​)=1+0=1.

Put these into a matrix (slide 3 makes this official):

CX​=[11​12​],ρX1​,X2​​=1⋅2​1​=2​1​≈0.71.

That's a pretty strong positive correlation, coming entirely from the shared Z1​.

Marginals. X1​=Z1​∼N(0,1). X2​=Z1​+Z2​ is a sum of independent normals, so X2​∼N(0,2) (L14 slide 5).

Joint pdf. The map (z1​,z2​)↦(x1​,x2​)=(z1​,z1​+z2​) can be undone: z1​=x1​ and z2​=x2​−x1​. So

P(X∈B)=P((Z1​,Z2​)∈{(x1​,x2​−x1​):(x1​,x2​)∈B}).

This map is a "shear": it slides points sideways without changing areas (its Jacobian, slide 7, is 1). So the density just gets carried along with no extra factor:

fX​(x1​,x2​)=fZ1​​(x1​)fZ2​​(x2​−x1​)=2π1​exp(−2x12​+(x2​−x1​)2​).

(L20 will show this is the bivariate normal density with covariance CX​. Quick check: CX−1​=[2−1​−11​] and xTCX−1​x=2x12​−2x1​x2​+x22​=x12​+(x2​−x1​)2. ✓)

Joint CDF. Condition on Z1​=z. Then X1​≤x1​ means z≤x1​, and X2​≤x2​ means Z2​≤x2​−z:

FX​(x1​,x2​)=P(Z1​≤x1​, Z1​+Z2​≤x2​)=∫−∞x1​​φ(z)P(Z2​≤x2​−z)dz=∫−∞x1​​φ(z)Φ(x2​−z)dz.

No closed form, and that's normal for vectors. Densities are usually much nicer to work with than CDFs once you have more than one variable.

Slide 2/36: Notation

On the slide. The CDF and pdf of X are FX​(x)=FX1​,…,Xn​​(x1​,…,xn​) and fX​(x)=fX1​,…,Xn​​(x1​,…,xn​). The joint CDF/pdf captures the correlation between components. The expected value vector is E[X]=(E[X1​],…,E[Xn​])T. Linearity of expectation holds here, so for any deterministic matrix A and vector b, and Y=AX+b, we have E[Y]=AE[X]+b.

Nothing new here, just shorthand:

FX​(x)=P(X1​≤x1​,…,Xn​≤xn​),P(X∈B)=∫B​fX​(x)dx.

The mean vector is just the vector of the individual means.

Why E[AX+b]=AE[X]+b. Look at one row at a time. The i-th component of Y is

Yi​=j∑​aij​Xj​+bi​,

an ordinary linear combination of random variables. By ordinary linearity, E[Yi​]=∑j​aij​E[Xj​]+bi​, which is exactly the i-th entry of AE[X]+b. Done. Note A can be any m×n matrix, so Y doesn't have to have the same length as X.

Marginals from the joint (recall L11). Integrate out everything you don't want:

fX1​​(x1​)=∫⋯∫fX​(x1​,x2​,…,xn​)dx2​⋯dxn​.

The joint determines the marginals, but not the other way round. The exception is independent components, where fX​=∏i​fXi​​.

Slide 3/36: The covariance matrix

On the slide. The covariance matrix CX​ captures the covariance between components and is defined by

CX​=E[(X−E[X])(X−E[X])T]=​Var(X1​)Cov(X2​,X1​)⋮Cov(Xn​,X1​)​Cov(X1​,X2​)Var(X2​)Cov(Xn​,X2​)​………​Cov(X1​,Xn​)Cov(X2​,Xn​)⋮Var(Xn​)​​

Why that outer product gives this matrix. Let D=X−E[X], a column vector (n×1). Then DDT is (n×1)(1×n)=n×n, and its (i,j) entry is

Di​Dj​=(Xi​−EXi​)(Xj​−EXj​).

Take expectations entry by entry and you get Cov(Xi​,Xj​). On the diagonal that's Cov(Xi​,Xi​)=Var(Xi​).

So CX​ is just "every covariance, arranged in a grid". It's the vector version of Var(X)=E[(X−EX)2].

Basic facts.

  • CX​ is symmetric, because Cov(Xi​,Xj​)=Cov(Xj​,Xi​).
  • Shortcut, like Var(X)=E[X2]−(EX)2:
CX​=E[XXT]−E[X]E[X]T.
  • Independent components give a diagonal CX​. The other way round fails in general (uncorrelated doesn't mean independent), but for Gaussian vectors it does hold (L20).
  • Correlation coefficients come straight from the entries: ρij​=Cii​Cjj​​Cij​​.

Slide 4/36: Properties, and functions of random vectors

On the slide. The covariance matrix CX​ is always positive semi-definite, i.e., for any vector a=0 we have aTCX​a≥0. Why? Let u=aT(X−E[X]); then aTCX​a=E[uuT]=E[u2]≥0. HW: if Y=AX+b, show that CY​=ACX​AT. Now recall how we obtained the pdf of Y from the pdf of X when Y=g(X): for g monotone, continuous and differentiable, fY​(y)=fX​(h(y))∣dydh​(y)∣ where h is the inverse function of g. How does this generalise to Y=G(X)? How do we get fY​ from fX​?

Positive semi-definite (PSD), in plain words. Pick any fixed vector a. Then aTX=∑i​ai​Xi​ is just one random variable, and its variance turns out to be

Var(aTX)=aTCX​a​

A variance can't be negative, so aTCX​a≥0 for every a. That's all PSD means here.

The slide's proof is exactly this. u=aT(X−EX) is a scalar with mean 0, so E[u2]=Var(aTX). And since u is a scalar, u2=uuT:

E[u2]=E[aT(X−EX)(X−EX)Ta]=aTE[(X−EX)(X−EX)T]a=aTCX​a.

(aT and a are constants, so they come out of the expectation by linearity.)

When is it strictly positive? aTCX​a=0 means Var(aTX)=0, so aTX is a constant. In other words, the components satisfy an exact linear relation.

Example (probabilitycourse 6.1.5). X,Y independent U(0,1) and V=(X,Y,X+Y)T. The third component is the sum of the first two, so a=(1,1,−1) gives aTV=0. Hence CV​ is singular, detCV​=0.

If there's no exact relation like that, CX​ is positive definite: all eigenvalues are >0, detCX​>0, and CX−1​ exists. L20's Gaussian density needs this inverse.

HW: CY​=ACX​AT. Since E[Y]=AE[X]+b, the b cancels when you centre:

Y−E[Y]=A(X−E[X]).

Now plug into the definition, using (AD)T=DTAT, and pull the constant matrices out:

CY​=E[A(X−EX)(X−EX)TAT]=AE[(X−EX)(X−EX)T]AT=ACX​AT.□
Y=AX+b ⟹ E[Y]=AE[X]+b,CY​=ACX​AT​

This is Var(aX+b)=a2Var(X) in matrix form: the shift b disappears, and A shows up "twice" (once on each side, playing the role of a2).

Two special cases worth knowing by heart (take A to be a single row):

Var(aTX)=aTCX​a,Cov(aTX,bTX)=aTCX​b.

Check with slide 1. There X=AZ with A=[11​01​] and CZ​=I. So CX​=AIAT=AAT=[11​12​]. ✓ Same answer as before, with no covariance algebra at all.

The 1D change of variables, recalled. For Y=g(X) with g monotone and h=g−1:

fY​(y)=fX​(h(y))∣h′(y)∣.

Think of ∣h′(y)∣ as a stretch factor. Probability is conserved: wherever g stretches intervals out, the same probability is spread over more room, so the density has to drop by the same factor. Slides 5 to 8 do the same in n dimensions. The derivative becomes a matrix of partial derivatives, and its determinant measures how volumes get stretched.

Slide 5/36: Functions of random vectors

On the slide. Let Y=G(X) where G:Rn→Rn is continuous and invertible with continuous partial derivatives. Then one can write Yi​=Gi​(X1​,…,Xn​) for i=1,…,n. For example, if [Y1​Y2​​]=[2X1​X1​+X2​​] then G1​(X1​,X2​)=2X1​ and G2​(X1​,X2​)=X1​+X2​. What does continuity of G mean? Continuity of components?

The blue question. A vector-valued function G=(G1​,…,Gn​) is continuous exactly when every component Gi​:Rn→R is continuous. That's because two vectors are close exactly when each coordinate is close. Same idea for "continuous partial derivatives": every ∂xj​∂Gi​​ has to exist and be continuous. In the example, G1​=2x1​ and G2​=x1​+x2​ are polynomials, so no problem.

Two things to check in every problem.

  1. Same dimension in and out (Rn→Rn). Otherwise the Jacobian matrix isn't square and has no determinant. What if you only want fewer variables, say just Y1​=X1​+X2​? Invent an extra one, like Y2​=X2​, use the theorem to get the joint density of (Y1​,Y2​), then integrate Y2​ out. (B12 does this.)
  2. Invertible (one-to-one), at least on the region where fX​>0. Each y must come from exactly one x.

Slide 6/36: The inverse map

On the slide. Let H denote the inverse of G. We similarly have Xi​=Hi​(Y1​,…,Yn​). For the example we have X1​=H1​(Y1​,Y2​)=2X1​​ [should read 2Y1​​] and X2​=H2​(Y1​,Y2​)=Y2​−2Y1​​.

Finding H = solving for the x's. From y1​=2x1​ we get x1​=2y1​​. Plug that into y2​=x1​+x2​ to get x2​=y2​−2y1​​. So

H(y)=[y1​/2y2​−y1​/2​].

(Typo on the slide: H1​ has to be written in terms of Y, so it's X1​=2Y1​​, not 2X1​​.)

Check: G(H(y))=(2⋅2y1​​, 2y1​​+y2​−2y1​​)=(y1​,y2​). ✓

Slide 7/36: The Jacobian theorem

On the slide. Let Y=G(X) where G:Rn→Rn is continuous and invertible with continuous partial derivatives, and let H denote its inverse. Then

fY​(y)=fX​(H(y))∣J∣

where J is the determinant of the Jacobian matrix

​∂y1​∂H1​​∂y1​∂H2​​⋮∂y1​∂Hn​​​∂y2​∂H1​​∂y2​∂H2​​∂y2​∂Hn​​​………​∂yn​∂H1​​∂yn​∂H2​​⋮∂yn​∂Hn​​​​
fY​(y)=fX​(H(y))∣J∣,J=det[∂yj​∂Hi​​]i,j​​

Compare with 1D: fX​(h(y)) becomes fX​(H(y)), and ∣h′(y)∣ becomes ∣J∣. Row i of the matrix is all the partial derivatives of the i-th inverse component Hi​.

Two things people mess up: J comes from the inverse map H (as a function of y), and the formula uses its absolute value.

The recipe.

  1. Solve y=G(x) for x=H(y).
  2. Write the matrix of partials of H and take its determinant J.
  3. Write fY​(y)=fX​(H(y))∣J∣.
  4. Find the support: all y for which H(y) lands where fX​>0. This is where most marks get lost, so don't skip it.

Shortcut. The Jacobian of the inverse is one over the Jacobian of the forward map:

J=det[∂Gi​/∂xj​]1​evaluated at x=H(y).

Use whichever one is easier to differentiate.

With n=1 the matrix is the single entry h′(y), and you get back the 1D formula from slide 4.

Slide 8/36: The Jacobian determinant, and two HWs

On the slide. From vector calculus: the Jacobian gives the ratio of the incremental areas dx1​dx2​⋯dxn​ and dy1​⋯dyn​. (Links: Wikipedia, Jacobian matrix and determinant; Khan Academy.) HW1: for the running example, find fY​(y). HW2: when Y=AX+b, show that fY​(y)=∣det(A)∣1​fX​(A−1(y−b)).

Why a determinant? (the "ratio of areas"). Probability is conserved. A tiny box dy around y comes from a tiny region dx around x=H(y), and both must carry the same probability:

fY​(y)vol(dy)=fX​(x)vol(dx)⟹fY​(y)=fX​(x)vol(dy)vol(dx)​.

Zoomed in close to y, the map H is basically linear, with matrix [∂yj​∂Hi​​]. And a linear map multiplies every volume by the absolute value of its determinant. So vol(dy)vol(dx)​=∣J∣.

Simplest case: [a0​0d​] turns a unit square into an a×d rectangle, area ∣ad∣, which is ∣det∣.

HW1: the running example. H(y)=(2y1​​, y2​−2y1​​). Partial derivatives, row by row:

[∂yj​∂Hi​​]=[21​−21​​01​],J=21​⋅1−0⋅(−21​)=21​.
fY​(y1​,y2​)=21​fX​(2y1​​, y2​−2y1​​)​

(Forward check: det[21​01​]=2, and 21​ is its reciprocal. G doubles areas, so the density gets halved.)

Plugging in specific X's.

  • X1​,X2​ i.i.d. N(0,1):
fY​(y)=4π1​exp(−21​[4y12​​+(y2​−2y1​​)2]).
  • X = slide 1's vector. There fX​(x1​,x2​)=2π1​exp(−21​[x12​+(x2​−x1​)2]), and x2​−x1​=y2​−y1​:
fY​(y)=4π1​exp(−21​[4y12​​+(y2​−y1​)2]).

Both are bivariate normal densities. With A=[21​01​] their covariance matrices are AAT=[42​22​] and ACX​AT=[44​45​]. Both have determinant 4, which matches the constant 2π4​1​=4π1​.

HW2: affine maps. Let A be an invertible n×n matrix. Solving y=Ax+b for x:

H(y)=A−1(y−b).

That's linear in y, and its matrix of partial derivatives is just the constant matrix A−1. So J=det(A−1)=detA1​, and

fY​(y)=∣detA∣1​fX​(A−1(y−b))​

(probabilitycourse Example 6.15.) The running example is the case A=[21​01​], detA=2, b=0. L20 uses exactly this formula, with X a standard normal vector, to get the multivariate Gaussian density.

Part B: extra worked examples and problems

General plan.

  • Mean / covariance of AX+b: AE[X]+b and ACX​AT. For a single entry, use aTCX​b instead of multiplying out the whole matrix.
  • Density of G(X): the four-step recipe from slide 7, and don't forget the support.
  • Density of one function of X: add a dummy variable, use the Jacobian, integrate the dummy out.

B1 (last year's HW9 Q3). Y1​=X1​+X2​, Y2​=X1​−X2​. (a) Find H. (b) Find ∣J∣. (c) Write fY​ in terms of fX​.

Solution

Solution. (a) Add the two equations: y1​+y2​=2x1​. Subtract: y1​−y2​=2x2​. So

X1​=2Y1​+Y2​​,X2​=2Y1​−Y2​​.

(b) J=det[21​21​​21​−21​​]=−41​−41​=−21​, so ∣J∣=21​. (c) fY​(y1​,y2​)=21​fX​(2y1​+y2​​,2y1​−y2​​).

Example. Take X1​,X2​ i.i.d. N(0,1). The exponent needs x12​+x22​, and

(2y1​+y2​​)2+(2y1​−y2​​)2=2y12​+y22​​

(the cross terms cancel). So

fY​(y)=21​⋅2π1​e−(y12​+y22​)/4=4π​1​e−y12​/4⋅4π​1​e−y22​/4.

It factorises, so the sum and difference are independent N(0,2) variables. That's special to normals; L20 explains why.

B2 (last year's Quiz 2 Q4). (X1​,X2​) uniform on the unit square, Y1​=X1​−X2​, Y2​=X1​+X2​. Find fY​.

Solution

Solution. Same kind of map as B1: X1​=2Y1​+Y2​​, X2​=2Y2​−Y1​​, ∣J∣=21​. Since fX​=1 on the square, fY​=21​ on the support, and 0 off it.

Now the important part, the support. We need 0<x1​<1 and 0<x2​<1:

0<2y1​+y2​​<1,0<2y2​−y1​​<1.

The two left inequalities say y2​>−y1​ and y2​>y1​, i.e. ∣y1​∣<y2​. The two right ones say y2​<2−y1​ and y2​<2+y1​, i.e. ∣y1​∣<2−y2​. Together:

∣y1​∣<y2​  (0<y2​≤1),∣y1​∣<2−y2​  (1<y2​<2).

That's a square with corners (0,0),(1,1),(0,2),(−1,1): the unit square rotated by 45° and scaled by 2​. Its area is 2, so the density 21​ integrates to 1. ✓

Cross-check. Integrate out y1​: at height y2​≤1 the width is 2y2​, so fY2​​(y2​)=21​⋅2y2​=y2​; for 1<y2​<2 it's 2−y2​. That's the triangle density of a sum of two uniforms, same as the L13 convolution.

B3 (last year's Tutorial 9 Q2): a non-linear map. X1​∼U[1,2] and, independently, X2​ has density 83​x22​ on [0,2]. Find the joint pdf of Y1​=X12​, Y2​=X1​+X2​.

Solution

Solution. Y1​=X12​ isn't one-to-one on all of R, but on the support X1​>0 it is, so we can take the positive root: X1​=Y1​​ and X2​=Y2​−Y1​​.

J=det[2y1​​1​−2y1​​1​​01​]=2y1​​1​.

fX1​​=1 on [1,2] and fX2​​(x2​)=83​x22​, so

fY​(y1​,y2​)=fX1​​(y1​​)fX2​​(y2​−y1​​)⋅2y1​​1​=1⋅83​(y2​−y1​​)2⋅2y1​​1​=16y1​​3(y2​−y1​​)2​.

Support: 1≤x1​≤2 means 1≤y1​≤4, and 0≤x2​≤2 means y1​​≤y2​≤y1​​+2. Zero elsewhere.

B4 (last year's Tutorial 9 Q1). X1​,X2​ independent with E[X1​]=2, Var(X1​)=4, E[X2​]=5, Var(X2​)=1. Y=AX with A=[13​2−1​]. Find E[Y] and CY​.

Solution

Solution. Mean: E[Y]=A[25​]=[2+106−5​]=[121​].

Covariance: independence gives CX​=diag(4,1). Multiply in two steps:

ACX​=[412​2−1​],CY​=ACX​AT=[412​2−1​][12​3−1​]=[810​1037​].

Check one entry by hand: Var(Y2​)=Var(3X1​−X2​)=9⋅4+1⋅1=37. ✓

B5 (last year's Tutorial 9 Q7). Show Var(aTX)=aTΣa and Cov(aTX,bTX)=aTΣb; evaluate for Σ=[41​12​], a=(2,−1)T, b=(1,3)T.

Solution

Solution. Stack the two rows into a 2×n matrix B=[aTbT​] and set Y=BX=(aTX,bTX)T. By slide 4's HW, CY​=BΣBT. Its (1,1) entry is aTΣa and its (1,2) entry is aTΣb. Done.

Numbers: Σa=(8−1,2−2)T=(7,0)T, so aTΣa=14. Σb=(4+3,1+6)T=(7,7)T, so aTΣb=2⋅7−1⋅7=7.

B6 (last year's HW9 Q7 and Q8). E[X]=(1,2)T, CX​=[41​12​]. (a) Y1​=2X1​−X2​+3, Y2​=X1​+4X2​. (b) Y1​=X1​+2X2​, Y2​=3X1​−X2​. Find the means and covariance matrices.

Solution

Solution. Use the single-entry formulas from B5, one row at a time.

(a) Mean: (2−2+3, 1+8)=(3,9). Rows a1​=(2,−1) and a2​=(1,4), so Σa1​=(7,0) and Σa2​=(8,9). Then

Var(Y1​)=a1T​Σa1​=14,Var(Y2​)=a2T​Σa2​=8+36=44,Cov=a1T​Σa2​=16−9=7,
CY​=[147​744​].

The +3 only shifts the mean, it doesn't touch the covariance.

(b) Mean: (1+4, 3−2)=(5,1). Rows (1,2) and (3,−1): Σ(1,2)T=(6,5) and Σ(3,−1)T=(11,1). So Var(Y1​)=6+10=16, Var(Y2​)=33−1=32, Cov=1⋅11+2⋅1=13:

CY​=[1613​1332​].

B7 (last year's HW9 Q1). Y=(Y1​,…,Y4​) with mean (5,−1,4,−3) and covariance diag(4,5,4,5). B=​2−10​−121​0−11​10−2​​. (a) E[BY]. (b) Cov(BY). (c) Which pairs have zero covariance?

Solution

Solution. (a) Bμ=(10+1+0−3, −5−2−4+0, 0−1+4+6)=(8,−11,9).

(b) With a diagonal Σ there's a nice shortcut: entry (i,j) of BΣBT is

k∑​Bik​Bjk​σk2​,

i.e. multiply row i and row j entry by entry, weight by the variances, and add. For example

(1,1)=22⋅4+12⋅5+0+12⋅5=26,(1,2)=(2)(−1)⋅4+(−1)(2)⋅5+0+0=−18.

Doing all of them:

BΣBT=​26−18−15​−18286​−15629​​.

(c) None. Every off-diagonal entry is nonzero.

B8 (last year's HW9 Q9). μ=(1,−1)T and Σ=[3−1​−12​]. Find E[(X1​+X2​)2].

Solution

Solution. X1​+X2​=aTX with a=(1,1)T. Use E[W2]=Var(W)+(EW)2:

Var(aTX)=aTΣa=3+2+2(−1)=3,aTμ=1−1=0.

So E[(X1​+X2​)2]=3+0=3.

B9 (probabilitycourse 6.1.5): a covariance matrix from a joint pdf. fX,Y​(x,y)=23​x2+y on (0,1)2. Find CU​ for U=(X,Y)T.

Solution

Solution. Marginals (integrate out the other variable):

fX​(x)=∫01​(23​x2+y)dy=23​x2+21​,fY​(y)=∫01​(23​x2+y)dx=y+21​.

Moments:

E[X]=85​,E[X2]=157​,E[Y]=127​,E[Y2]=125​,

and by LOTUS E[XY]=∫01​∫01​xy(23​x2+y)dxdy=4817​. Now variance = E[X2]−(EX)2, covariance = E[XY]−EXEY:

CU​=[157​−6425​⋅​4817​−9635​125​−14449​​]=[96073​−961​​−961​14411​​].

B10 (last year's Tutorial 9 Q8): the law of total covariance. (a) E[Y]=E[E[Y∣X]]. (b) Cov(Y)=E[ΣY∣X​]+Cov(μY∣X​). (c) For Y=AX+Z with X,Z independent, zero mean, covariances ΣX​,ΣZ​: find E[Y] and Cov(Y); evaluate for A=[10​21​], ΣX​=[41​13​], ΣZ​=diag(1,2).

Solution

Solution. (a) Iterated expectation (L12), one component at a time.

(b) This is L12's law of total variance in vector form. Split the deviation into "within" and "between" parts:

Y−EY=(Y−μY∣X​)+(μY∣X​−EY).

Take the outer product and the expectation. The first part squared gives E[ΣY∣X​], the second gives Cov(μY∣X​). The cross terms vanish, because given X, the second part is a constant and the first part has conditional mean 0.

(c) Given X, the only randomness left is Z. So μY∣X​=AX and ΣY∣X​=ΣZ​. Then E[Y]=AE[X]=0 and

Cov(Y)=ΣZ​+AΣX​AT.

Numbers: AΣX​=[61​73​], AΣX​AT=[207​73​], so

Cov(Y)=[217​75​].

B11 (probabilitycourse Ch. 14, Example 8): the Box–Muller method, proved with the Jacobian. Let U1​,U2​ be independent U(0,1) and

Z1​=−2lnU1​​cos(2πU2​),Z2​=−2lnU1​​sin(2πU2​).

Show that Z1​,Z2​ are independent N(0,1). (This is how you generate normal samples in practice, since L15's inverse transform has no closed form for the normal.)

Solution

Solution. Think polar: the radius is R=−2lnU1​​ and the angle is Θ=2πU2​. To invert, note r2=z12​+z22​=−2lnu1​, and the angle of (z1​,z2​) is 2πu2​:

u1​=e−(z12​+z22​)/2,u2​=2π1​θ(z1​,z2​).

Partial derivatives: ∂zi​∂u1​​=−zi​u1​, and for the angle, ∂z1​∂θ​=−r2z2​​, ∂z2​∂θ​=r2z1​​. So

J=det[−z1​u1​−2πr2z2​​​−z2​u1​2πr2z1​​​]=−2πr2u1​z12​​−2πr2u1​z22​​=−2πr2u1​(z12​+z22​)​=−2πu1​​.

fU​=1 on the unit square, so

fZ​(z1​,z2​)=1⋅∣J∣=2π1​e−(z12​+z22​)/2=φ(z1​)φ(z2​).

It factorises into two standard normal densities, so Z1​,Z2​ are independent N(0,1). □

B12: the density of a sum, via the "extra variable" trick. X1​,X2​ i.i.d. Exp(λ). Find the density of S=X1​+X2​ with the Jacobian method.

Solution

Solution. One output isn't enough for the theorem, so add a dummy: T=X1​. Inverting, X1​=T and X2​=S−T. In terms of (s,t):

J=det[∂s∂x1​​∂s∂x2​​​∂t∂x1​​∂t∂x2​​​]=det[01​1−1​]=−1,∣J∣=1.

So

fS,T​(s,t)=λe−λtλe−λ(s−t)=λ2e−λs,0<t<s

(the support is x1​>0, x2​>0, i.e. t>0 and s−t>0). Integrate the dummy out:

fS​(s)=∫0s​λ2e−λsdt=λ2se−λs,

the Gamma(2,λ) density. Same as L14 got with MGFs and L13 with convolution. In fact this trick reproduces the convolution formula in general.
